disease_info: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is characterized by persistent, excessive anxiety and worry about a variety of everyday events or activities, occurring more days than not for at least several months and typically lasting years if untreated. Individuals often describe the worry as difficult to control, and it is commonly accompanied by symptoms such as restlessness, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance. The disorder tends to have a chronic, fluctuating course, with periods of exacerbation linked to psychosocial stressors, and leads to significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. It is distinguished from normal worry by its pervasiveness, duration, intensity, and associated functional impairment, and from other anxiety or mood disorders by the breadth of worries rather than focus on specific fears, situations, or discrete episodes.

narrative.stressor: About a year and a half ago, Edelmira was promoted to lead a major digital preservation and community oral history initiative at her library, a role she had long wanted but that came with constant grant-writing deadlines, technology rollouts, and public expectations from the Mexican‑American community she serves. At the same time, budget uncertainties and a staffing freeze meant she was covering vacant positions, staying late to troubleshoot Alma and Koha issues, and postponing personal plans like her long‑imagined trips to Oaxaca and Kyoto. Over roughly a year, she noticed that her meticulous planning turned into near‑constant mental rehearsal of worst‑case scenarios about the project failing, donors pulling out, or letting down colleagues and elders who had entrusted their stories to the library, and she began skipping yoga classes, hikes, and social potlucks to keep reworking timelines and grant narratives. When she realized that her worry was intruding even into quiet moments in her garden and that she could no longer focus on reading or embroidery without her mind circling back to work, a colleague from her yoga group suggested she speak with a mental health professional, leading her to seek psychiatric care.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My mind just won’t stop going over everything that could go wrong at work, and I can’t seem to turn the worrying off anymore.”

narrative.stressor: Nicholas’s anxiety began to escalate after his divorce settlement two years ago left him with tighter finances just as he started seriously planning a community preschool venture and considering a transition into a curriculum specialist role. For the past year or so, he has been juggling his current teaching position, sketching business plans, and calculating retirement needs, all while watching rising living costs in Grand Rapids and wondering if he can keep his mortgage and fund the preschool dream. The combination of irregular income prospects, looming loans to start a school, and responsibility for his aging car and home repairs gradually turned his habitual future‑oriented mulling into a pervasive preoccupation with bills, what might happen if enrollment is low, and whether he will be able to support himself if he becomes ill or loses his job. When he found himself sitting in his garden unable to enjoy the plants he’d tended, repeatedly checking his bank account instead of practicing guitar, and making avoidant decisions about the preschool simply to quiet his financial fears, he brought it up to his primary care provider during a routine visit and was referred for psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I’m constantly worrying about money and my future, from the moment I wake up until I go to bed, and it’s taking over everything.”

narrative.stressor: Parin’s anxiety grew more clinically significant over the past year as several transitions converged: her youngest niece left for college, her ex‑husband remarried, and she began seriously contemplating scaling back her real estate work to prepare for retirement. The regional housing market became more volatile, with fluctuating interest rates and fewer listings, leaving her uncertain about her future income and whether she could maintain her current home and lifestyle in Bowling Green, especially as she prided herself on helping immigrant families find stability while feeling less certain about her own. She increasingly filled her schedule with mentoring younger agents, community cultural events, and additional listings, telling herself she was staying productive, but noticing that behind the busy calendar was a persistent sense that if she slowed down, she would lose control over her finances, social role, and identity as a high‑performing broker. When her concentration on contracts and negotiations began to slip and she caught herself rereading the same clauses repeatedly before closings, worried she might miss something critical, she became concerned that this mounting mental strain could jeopardize her professional reputation and finally agreed to see a psychiatrist after a close colleague gently pointed out the change.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I can’t seem to focus on my work the way I used to—my mind keeps drifting to everything that could go wrong, and I have to reread the same documents over and over.”
